text: He asks whether intermittent fasting is beneficial or unnecessary, noting that opinions about it differ.
He defines intermittent fasting as going without food for a set number of hours.
He says fasting periods may start at around four hours and extend to about sixteen hours, giving the body more time between meals.
He compares this pause to giving the body time to reset and process accumulated metabolic by-products.
He says that during fasting, the liver has time to use some of its stored fat.
He goes further and claims that intermittent fasting is a major treatment approach for fatty liver; this is his view rather than a universal medical conclusion.
He says intermittent fasting may help the liver reduce some of its stored energy reserves.
He describes the liver and muscles as drawing on stored glycogen and fat during fasting.
He says the body can then use stored materials as raw ingredients for normal metabolic processes.
He mentions the production of proteins and hormones and also refers to cortisol in the context of the body's internal regulation.
He suggests that fasting may help with some inflammatory or immune-related conditions, according to his approach.
He also says it may improve joint-pain symptoms and conditions resembling fibromyalgia, although he notes that the causes of such symptoms are not always clear.
He adds that symptoms resembling rheumatoid disease or skin allergies may also improve with intermittent fasting in his view.
He concludes that fasting correctly and breaking the fast correctly can, in his view, support better overall health.
